objectives.statement: Map sympathetic and parasympathetic anatomy, neurotransmitters and important sympathetic cholinergic exceptions.
Trace catecholamine synthesis and identify enzyme-level drug targets and false-transmitter mechanisms.
Explain vesicular storage, calcium-dependent release, neuronal reuptake and enzymatic metabolism of noradrenaline.
Analyse indirect sympathomimetics, monoamine-oxidase interactions and catecholamine-depleting drugs.
Relate alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptor location and signalling to ocular and systemic responses.
Relate beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3 receptor activation to target-organ responses and clinical use.
Select and compare phenylephrine, brimonidine and apraclonidine for appropriate ocular indications.
Compare alpha and beta antagonists by receptor selectivity, reversibility and therapeutic effect.
Recognize contraindications, systemic absorption risks and clinically important adverse effects of adrenergic drugs.
Integrate adrenergic receptor mechanisms with pupil, accommodation, aqueous dynamics and glaucoma treatment.
Trace acetylcholine synthesis, vesicular storage, release and enzymatic termination and identify relevant drug targets.
Distinguish muscarinic receptor signalling from neuronal and neuromuscular nicotinic receptor signalling.
Compare choline esters and alkaloid agonists by receptor selectivity, cholinesterase susceptibility and organ effects.
Apply pilocarpine and related muscarinic effects to pupil, accommodation and aqueous outflow.
Compare reversible and organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitors by duration, location and therapeutic use.
Recognize organophosphate toxicity and prioritize decontamination, airway support, atropine, pralidoxime and seizure control.
Predict ocular and systemic consequences of antimuscarinic drugs and select appropriate precautions.
Explain why ganglion stimulation or blockade produces variable organ responses based on prevailing autonomic tone.
Differentiate nondepolarizing from depolarizing neuromuscular blockade, reversal and safety risks.
Integrate cholinergic agonist and antagonist actions in ocular examination, glaucoma and patient counselling.

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub slide-aligned content team
questions.sampleAnswer: First protect staff and stop ongoing exposure, remove contaminated clothing and decontaminate while avoiding secondary contamination. Immediately support airway, oxygenation and ventilation because bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, CNS depression and neuromuscular weakness can all impair breathing. Give atropine and titrate to drying of dangerous bronchial secretions and improved ventilation rather than pupil size; atropine treats muscarinic effects but not nicotinic paralysis. Give pralidoxime early when organophosphate poisoning is suspected because it may reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before aging and improve weakness. Treat seizures with a benzodiazepine. Continuously monitor cardiac rhythm, oxygenation, secretions, temperature, weakness and recurrent toxicity, and involve toxicology/emergency expertise. Do not delay treatment for a cholinesterase result when the toxidrome is compelling.
rubric: Prioritizes responder safety, exposure termination and decontamination without delaying resuscitation.
Prioritizes airway, oxygenation and ventilatory support and explains the multiple causes of respiratory failure.
Explains that atropine treats muscarinic manifestations and is titrated to respiratory secretion/ventilation endpoints.
Explains that atropine does not reverse nicotinic weakness or regenerate acetylcholinesterase.
Explains the time-sensitive role and mechanism of pralidoxime before aging.
Includes benzodiazepine treatment for seizures and appropriate monitoring/reassessment.
Avoids unsafe claims such as neutralizing the pesticide chemically or waiting for laboratory confirmation before treatment.
